# Help the dead
## Every Ocean Hughes
Every Ocean Hughes is a transdisciplinary artist and writer. Spanning photography, sculpture, installation, performance, film, as well as writing and publishing, her practice manifests from an ongoing inquiry into performativity and the spaces that hold queer life, and, most recently, queer death. Collaboration is at the core of her work, for instance through the rich history of collaboration with LTTR, in addition to lyric writing, costume design, and curatorial projects.
Her recent solo exhibitions include Alive Time at Moderna Museet (Stockholm, 2022), One Big Bag at Studio Voltaire (London, 2022), Kunsthalle Lissabon (Lisbon, 2017), Secession (Vienna 2015), and PARTICIPANT INC, New York (2015). Hughes has presented commissions of new work at Tate Modern (London, 2012, 2017), the Stedelijk Museum (Amsterdam, 2014), Portland Institute of Contemporary Art (2014); and the Kitchen (New York 2010), among others.
She has also presented numerous projects in group exhibitions and festivals, including the Berlinale (2022), Witch Hunt at the Hammer Museum and ICA LA (Los Angeles, 2021), 11th Gwangju Biennale (2016); the Biennale of Sydney (2014); the Museum of Modern Art (New York, 2014); Future Generation Art Prize at the 55th Venice Biennale (2013); the Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía (Madrid, 2010); and the Whitney Biennial (New York, 2010). Hughes was a fellow at the Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study at Harvard University in 2019-2020. She is currently the Sachs Visiting Professor at University of Pennsylvania.
Every Ocean Hughes is based between Sweden and the United States. She is formerly known as Emily Roysdon.

# Jeppe Hein
Who are you really?
21.5–28.8 2022
Stockholm
Meet Jeppe Hein in the exhibition “Who are you really?” This summer, the Danish Berlin-based artist will engage the audience in totally new ways. The exhibition takes place around the entire Museum – both indoors and outdoors – and invites you to be a co-creator.
The extensive project “Jeppe Hein: Who are you really?” is not an exhibition in the traditional sense. Instead of shipping works to Moderna Museet, the entire exhibition was produced on site, interacting with the building, our collection – and our visitors.
> My artistic practice is about people, physical encounters, dialogue and social interaction. You viewers are an indispensable aspect of my art, and most of my installations can only be experienced if you are there – Jeppe Hein
Video 9
Jeppe Hein, Breath with me, 2022 Photo: Åsa Lunden / Moderna Museet
Video 10
texts.3:
# Jeppe Hein
### Indoors and outdoors
You will encounter Jeppe Hein’s art already on Exercisplan in front of the museum.
Play with the irregular patterns of water sprayed from the large fountain. See the wavy wall with the works “Breathe with Me”, previously shown at the UN Headquarters in New York in 2019, and “Today I Feel Like”.
texts.4:
# Jeppe Hein
### Participate in workshops
Indoors, in the Museum’s long collection corridor, Jeppe Hein has created a series of seven rooms that relate in colour and form to the seven chakras, used in yoga and other practises:
**I am, I feel, I do, I love, I speak, I see and I understand.**
Here, you can take part in simple workshops on the themes of each room.
Jeppe Hein, Breath with me, 2022 Photo: Åsa Lunden / Moderna Museet
Jeppe Hein, I feel, 2022 Photo: Åsa Lundén / Moderna Museet
Jeppe Hein, I love, 2022 Photo: Åsa Lundén / Moderna Museet
texts.5:
# Jeppe Hein
### Breath and mirrors
The third part of the exhibition consists of four spaces in The collection, where you are invited to join the workshops: “Today I feel like”, “Your mirror”, “Who are you really?” and “Breathe with me”.
By asking “Who are you really?” Jeppe Hein encourages visitors to interact and engage with the situations he stages.
Jeppe Hein, Your mirror, 2022 Photo: Åsa Lundén / Moderna Museet

The performance focuses on questions of self-determination, responsibility and the fantasy of continuity. The artist highlights death from a queer perspective. “Help the Dead” is about mutual aid and the social aspects of living and dying on Earth in our time.
This combined concert and theatre performance takes place on five occasions. The performers are Colin Self, artist, composer and choreographer, and Geo Wyeth, artist and educator.

# Help the dead
## Every Ocean Hughes
Every Ocean Hughes is a transdisciplinary artist and writer. Spanning photography, sculpture, installation, performance, film, as well as writing and publishing, her practice manifests from an ongoing inquiry into performativity and the spaces that hold queer life, and, most recently, queer death. Collaboration is at the core of her work, for instance through the rich history of collaboration with LTTR, in addition to lyric writing, costume design, and curatorial projects.
Her recent solo exhibitions include Alive Time at Moderna Museet (Stockholm, 2022), One Big Bag at Studio Voltaire (London, 2022), Kunsthalle Lissabon (Lisbon, 2017), Secession (Vienna 2015), and PARTICIPANT INC, New York (2015). Hughes has presented commissions of new work at Tate Modern (London, 2012, 2017), the Stedelijk Museum (Amsterdam, 2014), Portland Institute of Contemporary Art (2014); and the Kitchen (New York 2010), among others.
She has also presented numerous projects in group exhibitions and festivals, including the Berlinale (2022), Witch Hunt at the Hammer Museum and ICA LA (Los Angeles, 2021), 11th Gwangju Biennale (2016); the Biennale of Sydney (2014); the Museum of Modern Art (New York, 2014); Future Generation Art Prize at the 55th Venice Biennale (2013); the Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía (Madrid, 2010); and the Whitney Biennial (New York, 2010). Hughes was a fellow at the Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study at Harvard University in 2019-2020. She is currently the Sachs Visiting Professor at University of Pennsylvania.
Every Ocean Hughes is based between Sweden and the United States. She is formerly known as Emily Roysdon.

## Covid-19
In consultation with the other national museums, Moderna Museet in Stockholm and Malmö closed for the public on 22 March 2020 due to the covid pandemic. The museum adapted to the situation, and continued its efforts, to the extent that the restrictions allowed, to preserve the collection in the form of registering and conserving the art. New digital formats were launched to reach a large and broad public, and funding from private foundations were used to acquire Swedish contemporary art.
The exhibition “Giacometti – Face to Face” opened on 10 October, but the museum was forced to close again on 29 October. Malmö remained closed until 16 March 2022 and Stockholm until 25 March. During this closure, the museum continued to explore digital formats, such as live-broadcast “Sofa Tours”, workshops and “Create like…”
In 2021, Moderna Museet received a government allocation of SEK 25 million to support the Swedish arts sector during the covid-19 pandemic. Moderna Museet called this initiative “Swedish Acquisitions 2021”. The project resulted in 373 new works for the museum collection. They were made between 1962 and 2021 by 169 artists aged from 27 to 91 living in and outside Sweden and in Sápmi. The selection was shown in two exhibitions, “Insights” and “Matches”, in 2022.

## Covid-19
### A new manifesto
A comprehensive project involving the entire museum staff led to a manifesto that was announced by Gitte Ørskou in 2021. Moderna Museet should not distance itself from society but engage actively with the world, be inclusive and promote diversity, address a broader audience and embrace sustainable practices that take into account environmental and social impacts.
Just over a month after the Russian invasion of Ukraine, in February 2022, the museum in collaboration with Castello di Rivoli in Turin featured “A Letter from the Frontier” – 19 video works by 15 contemporary Ukrainian artists and artist groups, which could be viewed at the museum and on the Moderna Museet website.
texts.28:
## Covid-19
### Björn Lövin & Jeppe Hein
Throughout 2022, the museum paused all long-distance shipping of art. Among other things, this led to the exhibition “Björn Lövin – The Surrounding Reality”. None of Björn Lövin’s original so-called environments had been preserved since they were shown in the 1970s and 1980s, but three of them were reconstructed on site at the museum. Moderna Museet’s summer exhibition of Jeppe Hein was also produced on location, in interaction with visitors.
The year ended with a small exhibition of Hilma af Klint, attracting record visitor numbers.
texts.29:
## Covid-19
### New collection presentation
From 2023, Gitte Ørskou renewed the collection presentation through thematic exhibitions that made focused interventions across different periods and movements in 20th-century art. The first was “Sleepless Nights – From the 1980s in the Moderna Museet collection”. As part of the new presentation, artists such as Rashid Johnson and Maurizio Cattelan were also invited to select works from the collection.
Several artists were highlighted in solo exhibitions: Nan Goldin (2022), Laurie Anderson (2023), Lotte Laserstein (2023), Monica Sjöö (2023) and Britta Marakatt-Labba (2025).
At the end of 2025, Carsten Höller’s slides, “Stockholm Slides”, were installed on the museum’s façade, coinciding with the opening of a major Picasso exhibition featuring late works.
texts.30:
## Covid-19
### 2026 – Towards a new organisational structure
Moderna Museet is entering a new era of organisational change. In 2024, the Government decided to incorporate Statens konstråd and ArkDes into Moderna Museet. As of 1 January 2026, both institutions became part of the Moderna Museet government organisation.
Gitte Ørskou will leave her post in August 2026, and in September Tone Hansen will take up the position of Museum Director at Moderna Museet. Most recently, she served as Director of MUNCH in Oslo and previously led Henie Onstad Kunstsenter.

# Jeppe Hein
Who are you really?
21.5–28.8 2022
Stockholm
Meet Jeppe Hein in the exhibition “Who are you really?” This summer, the Danish Berlin-based artist will engage the audience in totally new ways. The exhibition takes place around the entire Museum – both indoors and outdoors – and invites you to be a co-creator.
The extensive project “Jeppe Hein: Who are you really?” is not an exhibition in the traditional sense. Instead of shipping works to Moderna Museet, the entire exhibition was produced on site, interacting with the building, our collection – and our visitors.
> My artistic practice is about people, physical encounters, dialogue and social interaction. You viewers are an indispensable aspect of my art, and most of my installations can only be experienced if you are there – Jeppe Hein

Jeppe Hein, Breath with me, 2022 Photo: Åsa Lunden / Moderna Museet

# Jeppe Hein
### Indoors and outdoors
You will encounter Jeppe Hein’s art already on Exercisplan in front of the museum.
Play with the irregular patterns of water sprayed from the large fountain. See the wavy wall with the works “Breathe with Me”, previously shown at the UN Headquarters in New York in 2019, and “Today I Feel Like”.

# Jeppe Hein
### Participate in workshops
Indoors, in the Museum’s long collection corridor, Jeppe Hein has created a series of seven rooms that relate in colour and form to the seven chakras, used in yoga and other practises:
**I am, I feel, I do, I love, I speak, I see and I understand.**
Here, you can take part in simple workshops on the themes of each room.
Jeppe Hein, Breath with me, 2022 Photo: Åsa Lunden / Moderna Museet
Jeppe Hein, I feel, 2022 Photo: Åsa Lundén / Moderna Museet
Jeppe Hein, I love, 2022 Photo: Åsa Lundén / Moderna Museet

# Jeppe Hein
### Breath and mirrors
The third part of the exhibition consists of four spaces in The collection, where you are invited to join the workshops: “Today I feel like”, “Your mirror”, “Who are you really?” and “Breathe with me”.
By asking “Who are you really?” Jeppe Hein encourages visitors to interact and engage with the situations he stages.

Events 2022
13.5 2022
Stockholm
Meet three artists from different generations, who were recently acquired within the framework of the Moderna Museet's major project for the acquisition of new art; “Swedish acquisitions 2021”. Listen to the artists Kristina Abelli Elander, Astrid Kajsa Nylander and Helena Lund Ek in a conversation about feminist art creation and the importance of predecessors and role models.
How do the possibilities of working as a woman and artist differ from the 1970s and 80s to today? How can one find strength and community in creation through networks?
Listen to the artists Kristina Abelli Elander, Astrid Kajsa Nylander and Helena Lund Ek in a conversation about feminist art creation and the importance of predecessors and role models. The conversation takes place in the exhibition “Swedish Acquisitions: Matches”, which opens on May 7, 2022. The exhibition is the second of two group exhibitions that present works from the Moderna Museet’s major project for acquiring new art “Swedish Acquisitions 2021”.
Kristina Abelli Elander started critiquing prevailing gender relations and social orders in her comicstrip-like paintings early on. Astrid Kajsa Nylander’s paintings often take on a surrealist expression departing from female artists’ work. In her work, Helena Lund Ek engages in dialogue with previous generations of artists and her figurative paintings are often about the body and the female experience.
The conversation is mediated by Linda Fagerström, lecturer in Art Theory at Linnaeus University.

## Conversation in Swedish acquisitions: Matches
### Date
Friday 13 May 2022

## Conversation in Swedish acquisitions: Matches
### Time

## Conversation in Swedish acquisitions: Matches
### Place
In the exhibition “Swedish acquisitions: Matches”, floor 2

## Conversation in Swedish acquisitions: Matches
### Language

## Conversation in Swedish acquisitions: Matches
### Registration information
Free admission. No pre-registration required
Contact: [Karin Malmquist](mailto:m.malmquist@modernamuseet.se), curator

## Astrid Kajsa Nylander
Astrid Kajsa Nylander received her MFA 2018 in Jutta Koether’s class for painting and drawing at the Hochschule für Bildende Künste Hamburg. In 2019, she was awarded the ‘Junge Kunst’ prize by the Stiftung Sparkasse Siegen, followed by a solo exhibition at the Siegen Kunstverein, Germany. In 2020, her mini-jobs were shown in a solo exhibition at the PAGE Gallery (NYC) in New York. Her solo exhibition “drip drop” opens on May 21, 2022 at Galleri Belenius in Stockholm.

## Helena Lund Ek
Helena Lund Ek graduated in 2014 from the Oslo Academy of the Arts and is currently a substitute lecturer in painting at the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts. Lund Ek participated in Modernautställningen in 2018 and has since initiated three site-specific solo exhibitions in Stockholm.
Together, Helena Lund Ek and Astrid Kajsa Nylander run Painting Practice, a collegial forum for painting with talks, exhibitions and workshops.

## Kristina Abelli Elander
Kristina Abelli Elander graduated from Birkagården’s one year textile programme in the early 1970s. She distinguished herself early on with comicstrip-like paintings that criticized prevailing social orders and gender balance. Over the years, she has worked using various methods; painting, drawing, textile sculpture, ceramics and spatial installations. She was also active as a costume designer during the 1970s to 1990s.
In the early 1980s, Abelli Elander was involved in running the legendary BarBar, an experimental alternative venue for new art forms. During the 1990s and 2000s, she taught at Konstfack and was a visiting professor at the Royal Swedish of Fine Arts.
For the past two years, Abelli Elander’s focus has been on animation and short films. Among her publications ”Staden, flickorna, Tiden…tiden…” (2011) can be mentioned.

## Linda Fagerström
Linda Fagerström is a lecturer in Art Theory at Linnaeus University and an art critic for Sydsvenskan. She is also chair of the Swedish Art Critics Association, AICA Sweden. As a researcher, Fagerström is interested in the polyphonic, and is strongly convinced that a story or a truth is never the only one. For her, gender perspective is an obvious point of departure.

**Moderna Museet** has one of the world’s finest collections of 20th and 21st century art. The photography collection goes back as far as 1840. Moderna Museet is commissioned to collect, preserve, exhibit and organise learning activities relating to all forms of 20th and 21st century art.
**Moderna Museet** in Stockholm originally opened on 9 May, 1958, in what used to be a drill hall on Skeppsholmen. The Spanish architect Rafael Moneo designed the new building for Moderna Museet, after winning an international competition for the assignment. The new building was inaugurated, according to plan, in connection with Stockholm Cultural Capital in 1998. The event took place on 12 February, 1998.
The museum houses Swedish and international modern and contemporary art, including pieces by Pablo Picasso and Salvador Dalí and a model of the Tatlin’s Tower. The museum’s collection includes also key works by artists such as Marcel Duchamp, Louise Bourgeois, Niki de Saint Phalle, Henri Matisse and Robert Rauschenberg, as well as ongoing acquisitions by contemporary artists.

## Covid-19
In consultation with the other national museums, Moderna Museet in Stockholm and Malmö closed for the public on 22 March 2020 due to the covid pandemic. The museum adapted to the situation, and continued its efforts, to the extent that the restrictions allowed, to preserve the collection in the form of registering and conserving the art. New digital formats were launched to reach a large and broad public, and funding from private foundations were used to acquire Swedish contemporary art.
The exhibition “Giacometti – Face to Face” opened on 10 October, but the museum was forced to close again on 29 October. Malmö remained closed until 16 March 2022 and Stockholm until 25 March. During this closure, the museum continued to explore digital formats, such as live-broadcast “Sofa Tours”, workshops and “Create like…”
In 2021, Moderna Museet received a government allocation of SEK 25 million to support the Swedish arts sector during the covid-19 pandemic. Moderna Museet called this initiative “Swedish Acquisitions 2021”. The project resulted in 373 new works for the museum collection. They were made between 1962 and 2021 by 169 artists aged from 27 to 91 living in and outside Sweden and in Sápmi. The selection was shown in two exhibitions, “Insights” and “Matches”, in 2022.

## Covid-19
### A new manifesto
A comprehensive project involving the entire museum staff led to a manifesto that was announced by Gitte Ørskou in 2021. Moderna Museet should not distance itself from society but engage actively with the world, be inclusive and promote diversity, address a broader audience and embrace sustainable practices that take into account environmental and social impacts.
Just over a month after the Russian invasion of Ukraine, in February 2022, the museum in collaboration with Castello di Rivoli in Turin featured “A Letter from the Frontier” – 19 video works by 15 contemporary Ukrainian artists and artist groups, which could be viewed at the museum and on the Moderna Museet website.

## Covid-19
### Björn Lövin & Jeppe Hein
Throughout 2022, the museum paused all long-distance shipping of art. Among other things, this led to the exhibition “Björn Lövin – The Surrounding Reality”. None of Björn Lövin’s original so-called environments had been preserved since they were shown in the 1970s and 1980s, but three of them were reconstructed on site at the museum. Moderna Museet’s summer exhibition of Jeppe Hein was also produced on location, in interaction with visitors.
The year ended with a small exhibition of Hilma af Klint, attracting record visitor numbers.

## Covid-19
### New collection presentation
From 2023, Gitte Ørskou renewed the collection presentation through thematic exhibitions that made focused interventions across different periods and movements in 20th-century art. The first was “Sleepless Nights – From the 1980s in the Moderna Museet collection”. As part of the new presentation, artists such as Rashid Johnson and Maurizio Cattelan were also invited to select works from the collection.
Several artists were highlighted in solo exhibitions: Nan Goldin (2022), Laurie Anderson (2023), Lotte Laserstein (2023), Monica Sjöö (2023) and Britta Marakatt-Labba (2025).
At the end of 2025, Carsten Höller’s slides, “Stockholm Slides”, were installed on the museum’s façade, coinciding with the opening of a major Picasso exhibition featuring late works.

## Covid-19
### 2026 – Towards a new organisational structure
Moderna Museet is entering a new era of organisational change. In 2024, the Government decided to incorporate Statens konstråd and ArkDes into Moderna Museet. As of 1 January 2026, both institutions became part of the Moderna Museet government organisation.
Gitte Ørskou will leave her post in August 2026, and in September Tone Hansen will take up the position of Museum Director at Moderna Museet. Most recently, she served as Director of MUNCH in Oslo and previously led Henie Onstad Kunstsenter.

Meet three artists from different generations, who were recently acquired within the framework of the Moderna Museet's major project for the acquisition of new art; “Swedish acquisitions 2021”. Listen to the artists Kristina Abelli Elander, Astrid Kajsa Nylander and Helena Lund Ek in a conversation about feminist art creation and the importance of predecessors and role models.
How do the possibilities of working as a woman and artist differ from the 1970s and 80s to today? How can one find strength and community in creation through networks?
Listen to the artists Kristina Abelli Elander, Astrid Kajsa Nylander and Helena Lund Ek in a conversation about feminist art creation and the importance of predecessors and role models. The conversation takes place in the exhibition “Swedish Acquisitions: Matches”, which opens on May 7, 2022. The exhibition is the second of two group exhibitions that present works from the Moderna Museet’s major project for acquiring new art “Swedish Acquisitions 2021”.
Kristina Abelli Elander started critiquing prevailing gender relations and social orders in her comicstrip-like paintings early on. Astrid Kajsa Nylander’s paintings often take on a surrealist expression departing from female artists’ work. In her work, Helena Lund Ek engages in dialogue with previous generations of artists and her figurative paintings are often about the body and the female experience.

## Astrid Kajsa Nylander
Astrid Kajsa Nylander received her MFA 2018 in Jutta Koether’s class for painting and drawing at the Hochschule für Bildende Künste Hamburg. In 2019, she was awarded the ‘Junge Kunst’ prize by the Stiftung Sparkasse Siegen, followed by a solo exhibition at the Siegen Kunstverein, Germany. In 2020, her mini-jobs were shown in a solo exhibition at the PAGE Gallery (NYC) in New York. Her solo exhibition “drip drop” opens on May 21, 2022 at Galleri Belenius in Stockholm.

## Helena Lund Ek
Helena Lund Ek graduated in 2014 from the Oslo Academy of the Arts and is currently a substitute lecturer in painting at the Royal Swedish Academy of Fine Arts. Lund Ek participated in Modernautställningen in 2018 and has since initiated three site-specific solo exhibitions in Stockholm.
Together, Helena Lund Ek and Astrid Kajsa Nylander run Painting Practice, a collegial forum for painting with talks, exhibitions and workshops.

## Kristina Abelli Elander
Kristina Abelli Elander graduated from Birkagården’s one year textile programme in the early 1970s. She distinguished herself early on with comicstrip-like paintings that criticized prevailing social orders and gender balance. Over the years, she has worked using various methods; painting, drawing, textile sculpture, ceramics and spatial installations. She was also active as a costume designer during the 1970s to 1990s.
In the early 1980s, Abelli Elander was involved in running the legendary BarBar, an experimental alternative venue for new art forms. During the 1990s and 2000s, she taught at Konstfack and was a visiting professor at the Royal Swedish of Fine Arts.
For the past two years, Abelli Elander’s focus has been on animation and short films. Among her publications ”Staden, flickorna, Tiden…tiden…” (2011) can be mentioned.

## Linda Fagerström
Linda Fagerström is a lecturer in Art Theory at Linnaeus University and an art critic for Sydsvenskan. She is also chair of the Swedish Art Critics Association, AICA Sweden. As a researcher, Fagerström is interested in the polyphonic, and is strongly convinced that a story or a truth is never the only one. For her, gender perspective is an obvious point of departure.

**Moderna Museet** has one of the world’s finest collections of 20th and 21st century art. The photography collection goes back as far as 1840. Moderna Museet is commissioned to collect, preserve, exhibit and organise learning activities relating to all forms of 20th and 21st century art.

The new building was inaugurated, according to plan, in connection with Stockholm Cultural Capital in 1998. The event took place on 12 February, 1998.
The museum houses Swedish and international modern and contemporary art, including pieces by Pablo Picasso and Salvador Dalí and a model of the Tatlin’s Tower. The museum’s collection includes also key works by artists such as Marcel Duchamp, Louise Bourgeois, Niki de Saint Phalle, Henri Matisse and Robert Rauschenberg, as well as ongoing acquisitions by contemporary artists.

## 2000s
### The new refurbished Moderna Museet
On 14 February 2004, the museum building reopened with a big celebration. In addition to repairs, the opportunity was taken to improve certain areas, partly to help visitor flows and to use the front entrance area better. The graphic profile was also updated.
Alongside the first exhibitions, “The Pontus Hultén Collection…” and “Anna Riwkin – a Portrait of a Photographer”, a major initiative focused on a presentation of the collection, called “In Our Time”. Works from 1900 to 2004 were arranged in reverse chronological order, so that visitors encountered contemporary art first, before walking back a hundred years in time to the far end of the building.

## 2000s
### The 1st at Moderna
Another significant change at the reopening was the introduction of hosts – staff with skills ranging from first aid to providing information about individual works and the current exhibitions. The hosts were employed to cater for the large increase in visitors when the free admission reform was introduced in 2005, making it free to visit the collection and some temporary exhibitions.
The admission fee was reintroduced in 2007, only to be removed again on 1 February 2016. Admission was free until 31 December 2022, when all national museums again had to charge admission.
An exhibition series called “The 1st at Moderna” was launched in 2004. On the first day of each month, a smaller exhibition opened somewhere in the museum. A total of 58 exhibitions were held in this series until it ended in 2008. That year, the British-Nigerian artist Yinka Shonibare covered parts of the museum’s public walls with fabric, as a four-year exhibition project.

## 2000s
### Robert Rauschenberg, Andy Warhol & Lee Lozano
In the decade following the reopening, the museum featured numerous exhibitions that got wide media attention, including Edvard Munch, Paul McCarthy, Robert Rauschenberg, Andy Warhol, Lee Lozano and Ed Ruscha, and several group exhibitions, such as “Africa Remix”, “Dalí Dalí with Francesco Vezzoli” and “Turner, Monet, Twombly”. Also, the Moderna Exhibition was introduced, with its four-yearly reviews of Swedish contemporary art, and “Time & Place”, three consecutive exhibitions featuring Los Angeles in 1957 – 1968, Milan/Turin in 1958 – 1968 and Rio de Janeiro in 1956 – 1964. In 2008, the wall project by Yinka Shonibare was replaced by Barbara Kruger’s characteristic graphic slogans on social issues.
Moderna Museet Malmö, 2012 Photo: Åsa Lundén/Moderna Museet

## Moderna Museet Malmö
In 1901, the architect John Smedberg designed a beautiful power station on Gasverksgatan 22, with a bright, shining gasometer that guaranteed the citizens of Malmö that they would have electricity. Just over a century later, the building – and the whole neighbourhood – had changed. After the popular art museum Rooseum closed, the premises were offered to Moderna Museet. In 2008, It was decided that Moderna Museet in Stockholm would open a branch in Malmö, in one of Sweden’s most beautiful exhibition spaces. Once more, the old power station would be filled with art.

## Moderna Museet Malmö
### Opened on 26 December 2009
The assignment to convert the building into a more functional museum went to Tham & Videgård Hansson Arkitekter. They chose to create a new annexe – a contemporary addition to the historical building. They also changed the floor plan of the existing premises. On 26 December, 2009, Moderna Museet Malmö opened. The then curator at Dunkers Kulturhus in Helsingborg, Magnus Jensner, had been appointed director of the museum the previous year, a position he held until 1 March 2012. He was succeeded by the former curators at Moderna Museet in Stockholm, John Peter Nilsson (2012 – 2016) and Iris Müller-Westermann (2017 – 2022).
On 22 August 2022, Elisabeth Millqvist became the director of Moderna Museet Malmö. She had been the artistic director and head of operations at Wanås Konst since 2011.

## 2010s
In November 2010, Daniel Birnbaum became the new chief curator and director of Moderna Museet. Daniel Birnbaum was formerly the vice-chancellor and a professor at Städelschule in Frankfurt, Germany, and the chief curator of numerous major international exhibitions and biennials, including the Venice Biennale in 2009.
In 2011, the exhibition series “Moment” replaces the previous “The 1st at Moderna”, as a forum for smaller exhibitions dotted around the museum. That year, a comprehensive reshuffling began in the presentation of the Moderna Museet collection.
Under the umbrella banner of “Another Story”, the museum showed only photography, from the 1840s to the early 2000s, from its own collection of some 100,000 photographs. This radical re-hanging was presented in the collection galleries throughout 2011.

## 2010s
### International group exhibitions
In Stockholm, the exhibition programme in the 2010s was predominantly female: Eva Löfdahl, Eija-Liisa Ahtila, Yoko Ono, Yayoi Kusama, Marina Abramovic, Cindy Sherman and Marie-Louise Ekman were a few of the artists featured.
Among the notable international group exhibitions were “Explosion – Painting as Action”, “Pop Art Design” and “Sculpture after Sculpture”, along with mid-career exhibitions of Wolfgang Tillmans and Olafur Eliasson. In February 2012, the museum stayed open for 48 hours for the sound installation “freq_out 8”.

## 2010s
### Hilma af Klint, Hannah Ryggen & Rosemarie Trockel
Women artists were also highlighted at Moderna Museet Malmö in the 2010s, including Doris Salcedo, Tala Madani, Tora Vega Holmström, Hannah Ryggen, Rosemarie Trockel and Hilma af Klint.
In association with Moderna Museet in Stockholm, several exhibitions of works from the collection were featured, including “Supersurrealism”, “Towards a Bigger World” and “A Way of Life”, along with international group shows such as “The New Human” and solo presentations of artists such as Ragnar Kjartansson and Katarzyna Kobro & Władysław Strzemiński. One of the public favourites was “ACTIONPAINTINGBABYSPLASH!”, an experimental mixture of exhibition and creative workshop in 2015.
On 31 December 2018, Daniel Birnbaum resigned as director of Moderna Museet, and Ann-Sofi Noring took over as acting director. Noring’s directorship ended on 1 September 2019, when she was succeeded by Gitte Ørskou, who had been the director of the Kunsten Museum of Modern Art in Aalborg, Denmark, since 2009. Before that, she was the curator and chief curator of ARoS Aarhus Kunstmuseum. She had also been on several boards, and chaired the Danish Arts Foundation.

# The Film Club: One Big Bag
Film & Discussion
25.3 2022
Stockholm
The Film Club welcomes you to an evening with the artist Every Ocean Hughes and her film “One Big Bag” (2021), which is a part of the exhibition “Alive Time”. See the film on the big screen, and have a discussion with the artist in the Q & A following the screening, which is led by the curator Mason Leaver-Yap.
The script of “One Big Bag” is drawn from workshops, research and interviews Every Ocean Hughes conducted with several end-of-life doulas from different cultural backgrounds. ## 2000s
### The new refurbished Moderna Museet
On 14 February 2004, the museum building reopened with a big celebration. In addition to repairs, the opportunity was taken to improve certain areas, partly to help visitor flows and to use the front entrance area better. The graphic profile was also updated.
Alongside the first exhibitions, “The Pontus Hultén Collection…” and “Anna Riwkin – a Portrait of a Photographer”, a major initiative focused on a presentation of the collection, called “In Our Time”. Works from 1900 to 2004 were arranged in reverse chronological order, so that visitors encountered contemporary art first, before walking back a hundred years in time to the far end of the building.
texts.18:
## 2000s
### The 1st at Moderna
Another significant change at the reopening was the introduction of hosts – staff with skills ranging from first aid to providing information about individual works and the current exhibitions. The hosts were employed to cater for the large increase in visitors when the free admission reform was introduced in 2005, making it free to visit the collection and some temporary exhibitions.
The admission fee was reintroduced in 2007, only to be removed again on 1 February 2016. Admission was free until 31 December 2022, when all national museums again had to charge admission.
An exhibition series called “The 1st at Moderna” was launched in 2004. On the first day of each month, a smaller exhibition opened somewhere in the museum. A total of 58 exhibitions were held in this series until it ended in 2008. That year, the British-Nigerian artist Yinka Shonibare covered parts of the museum’s public walls with fabric, as a four-year exhibition project.
texts.19:
## 2000s
### Robert Rauschenberg, Andy Warhol & Lee Lozano
In the decade following the reopening, the museum featured numerous exhibitions that got wide media attention, including Edvard Munch, Paul McCarthy, Robert Rauschenberg, Andy Warhol, Lee Lozano and Ed Ruscha, and several group exhibitions, such as “Africa Remix”, “Dalí Dalí with Francesco Vezzoli” and “Turner, Monet, Twombly”. Also, the Moderna Exhibition was introduced, with its four-yearly reviews of Swedish contemporary art, and “Time & Place”, three consecutive exhibitions featuring Los Angeles in 1957 – 1968, Milan/Turin in 1958 – 1968 and Rio de Janeiro in 1956 – 1964. In 2008, the wall project by Yinka Shonibare was replaced by Barbara Kruger’s characteristic graphic slogans on social issues.
Moderna Museet Malmö, 2012 Photo: Åsa Lundén/Moderna Museet
texts.20:
## Moderna Museet Malmö
In 1901, the architect John Smedberg designed a beautiful power station on Gasverksgatan 22, with a bright, shining gasometer that guaranteed the citizens of Malmö that they would have electricity. Just over a century later, the building – and the whole neighbourhood – had changed. After the popular art museum Rooseum closed, the premises were offered to Moderna Museet. In 2008, It was decided that Moderna Museet in Stockholm would open a branch in Malmö, in one of Sweden’s most beautiful exhibition spaces. Once more, the old power station would be filled with art.
texts.21:
## Moderna Museet Malmö
### Opened on 26 December 2009
The assignment to convert the building into a more functional museum went to Tham & Videgård Hansson Arkitekter. They chose to create a new annexe – a contemporary addition to the historical building. They also changed the floor plan of the existing premises. On 26 December, 2009, Moderna Museet Malmö opened. The then curator at Dunkers Kulturhus in Helsingborg, Magnus Jensner, had been appointed director of the museum the previous year, a position he held until 1 March 2012. He was succeeded by the former curators at Moderna Museet in Stockholm, John Peter Nilsson (2012 – 2016) and Iris Müller-Westermann (2017 – 2022).
On 22 August 2022, Elisabeth Millqvist became the director of Moderna Museet Malmö. She had been the artistic director and head of operations at Wanås Konst since 2011.
texts.22:
## 2010s
In November 2010, Daniel Birnbaum became the new chief curator and director of Moderna Museet. Daniel Birnbaum was formerly the vice-chancellor and a professor at Städelschule in Frankfurt, Germany, and the chief curator of numerous major international exhibitions and biennials, including the Venice Biennale in 2009.
In 2011, the exhibition series “Moment” replaces the previous “The 1st at Moderna”, as a forum for smaller exhibitions dotted around the museum. That year, a comprehensive reshuffling began in the presentation of the Moderna Museet collection.
Under the umbrella banner of “Another Story”, the museum showed only photography, from the 1840s to the early 2000s, from its own collection of some 100,000 photographs. This radical re-hanging was presented in the collection galleries throughout 2011.
texts.23:
## 2010s
### International group exhibitions
In Stockholm, the exhibition programme in the 2010s was predominantly female: Eva Löfdahl, Eija-Liisa Ahtila, Yoko Ono, Yayoi Kusama, Marina Abramovic, Cindy Sherman and Marie-Louise Ekman were a few of the artists featured.
Among the notable international group exhibitions were “Explosion – Painting as Action”, “Pop Art Design” and “Sculpture after Sculpture”, along with mid-career exhibitions of Wolfgang Tillmans and Olafur Eliasson. In February 2012, the museum stayed open for 48 hours for the sound installation “freq_out 8”.
texts.24:
## 2010s
### Hilma af Klint, Hannah Ryggen & Rosemarie Trockel
Women artists were also highlighted at Moderna Museet Malmö in the 2010s, including Doris Salcedo, Tala Madani, Tora Vega Holmström, Hannah Ryggen, Rosemarie Trockel and Hilma af Klint.
In association with Moderna Museet in Stockholm, several exhibitions of works from the collection were featured, including “Supersurrealism”, “Towards a Bigger World” and “A Way of Life”, along with international group shows such as “The New Human” and solo presentations of artists such as Ragnar Kjartansson and Katarzyna Kobro & Władysław Strzemiński. One of the public favourites was “ACTIONPAINTINGBABYSPLASH!”, an experimental mixture of exhibition and creative workshop in 2015.
On 31 December 2018, Daniel Birnbaum resigned as director of Moderna Museet, and Ann-Sofi Noring took over as acting director. Noring’s directorship ended on 1 September 2019, when she was succeeded by Gitte Ørskou, who had been the director of the Kunsten Museum of Modern Art in Aalborg, Denmark, since 2009. Before that, she was the curator and chief curator of ARoS Aarhus Kunstmuseum. She had also been on several boards, and chaired the Danish Arts Foundation.
texts.26:
## Covid-19
In consultation with the other national museums, Moderna Museet in Stockholm and Malmö closed for the public on 22 March 2020 due to the covid pandemic. The museum adapted to the situation, and continued its efforts, to the extent that the restrictions allowed, to preserve the collection in the form of registering and conserving the art. New digital formats were launched to reach a large and broad public, and funding from private foundations were used to acquire Swedish contemporary art.
The exhibition “Giacometti – Face to Face” opened on 10 October, but the museum was forced to close again on 29 October. Malmö remained closed until 16 March 2022 and Stockholm until 25 March. During this closure, the museum continued to explore digital formats, such as live-broadcast “Sofa Tours”, workshops and “Create like…”
In 2021, Moderna Museet received a government allocation of SEK 25 million to support the Swedish arts sector during the covid-19 pandemic. Moderna Museet called this initiative “Swedish Acquisitions 2021”. The project resulted in 373 new works for the museum collection. They were made between 1962 and 2021 by 169 artists aged from 27 to 91 living in and outside Sweden and in Sápmi. The selection was shown in two exhibitions, “Insights” and “Matches”, in 2022.
texts.27:
## Covid-19
### A new manifesto
A comprehensive project involving the entire museum staff led to a manifesto that was announced by Gitte Ørskou in 2021. # The Film Club: One Big Bag
Film & Discussion
25.3 2022
Stockholm
The Film Club welcomes you to an evening with the artist Every Ocean Hughes and her film “One Big Bag” (2021), which is a part of the exhibition “Alive Time”. See the film on the big screen, and have a discussion with the artist in the Q & A following the screening, which is led by the curator Mason Leaver-Yap.
The script of “One Big Bag” is drawn from workshops, research and interviews Every Ocean Hughes conducted with several end-of-life doulas from different cultural backgrounds. The video uses the “mobile corpse kit – a bag filled with everyday objects doulas use to care for the newly dead – as both the visual structure and narrative driver of the video.
With a matter-of-fact-demeanour and intense physicality, the performer guides the viewer into the largely uncharted waters of corpse care – practical, political and spiritual. The form of the video creates a tension between the subject matter of dying and the forceful aliveness of the performance itself.
The screening is followed by a conversation between Every Ocean Hughes and the curator Mason Leaver-Yap, who through earlier collaborations is intimately familiar with the artist’s work.

# The Film Club: One Big Bag
## Every Ocean Hughes
Every Ocean Hughes is a transdisciplinary artist and writer. Spanning photography, sculpture, installation, performance, film, as well as writing and publishing, her practice manifests from an ongoing inquiry into performativity and the spaces that hold queer life, and, most recently, queer death. Collaboration is at the core of her work, for instance through the rich history of collaboration with LTTR, in addition to lyric writing, costume design, and curatorial projects.
Her recent solo exhibitions include Alive Time at Moderna Museet (Stockholm, 2022), One Big Bag at Studio Voltaire (London, 2022), Kunsthalle Lissabon (Lisbon, 2017), Secession (Vienna 2015), and PARTICIPANT INC, New York (2015). Hughes has presented commissions of new work at Tate Modern (London, 2012, 2017), the Stedelijk Museum (Amsterdam, 2014), Portland Institute of Contemporary Art (2014); and the Kitchen (New York 2010), among others.
She has also presented numerous projects in group exhibitions and festivals, including the Berlinale (2022), Witch Hunt at the Hammer Museum and ICA LA (Los Angeles, 2021), 11th Gwangju Biennale (2016); the Biennale of Sydney (2014); the Museum of Modern Art (New York, 2014); Future Generation Art Prize at the 55th Venice Biennale (2013); the Museo Nacional Centro de Arte Reina Sofía (Madrid, 2010); and the Whitney Biennial (New York, 2010). Hughes was a fellow at the Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study at Harvard University in 2019-2020. She is currently the Sachs Visiting Professor at University of Pennsylvania.
Every Ocean Hughes is based between Sweden and the United States. She is formerly known as Emily Roysdon.

## 2000s
### The new refurbished Moderna Museet
On 14 February 2004, the museum building reopened with a big celebration. In addition to repairs, the opportunity was taken to improve certain areas, partly to help visitor flows and to use the front entrance area better. The graphic profile was also updated.
Alongside the first exhibitions, “The Pontus Hultén Collection…” and “Anna Riwkin – a Portrait of a Photographer”, a major initiative focused on a presentation of the collection, called “In Our Time”. Works from 1900 to 2004 were arranged in reverse chronological order, so that visitors encountered contemporary art first, before walking back a hundred years in time to the far end of the building.

## 2000s
### The 1st at Moderna
Another significant change at the reopening was the introduction of hosts – staff with skills ranging from first aid to providing information about individual works and the current exhibitions. The hosts were employed to cater for the large increase in visitors when the free admission reform was introduced in 2005, making it free to visit the collection and some temporary exhibitions.
The admission fee was reintroduced in 2007, only to be removed again on 1 February 2016. Admission was free until 31 December 2022, when all national museums again had to charge admission.
An exhibition series called “The 1st at Moderna” was launched in 2004. On the first day of each month, a smaller exhibition opened somewhere in the museum. A total of 58 exhibitions were held in this series until it ended in 2008. That year, the British-Nigerian artist Yinka Shonibare covered parts of the museum’s public walls with fabric, as a four-year exhibition project.

## 2000s
### Robert Rauschenberg, Andy Warhol & Lee Lozano
In the decade following the reopening, the museum featured numerous exhibitions that got wide media attention, including Edvard Munch, Paul McCarthy, Robert Rauschenberg, Andy Warhol, Lee Lozano and Ed Ruscha, and several group exhibitions, such as “Africa Remix”, “Dalí Dalí with Francesco Vezzoli” and “Turner, Monet, Twombly”. Also, the Moderna Exhibition was introduced, with its four-yearly reviews of Swedish contemporary art, and “Time & Place”, three consecutive exhibitions featuring Los Angeles in 1957 – 1968, Milan/Turin in 1958 – 1968 and Rio de Janeiro in 1956 – 1964. In 2008, the wall project by Yinka Shonibare was replaced by Barbara Kruger’s characteristic graphic slogans on social issues.
Moderna Museet Malmö, 2012 Photo: Åsa Lundén/Moderna Museet

## Moderna Museet Malmö
In 1901, the architect John Smedberg designed a beautiful power station on Gasverksgatan 22, with a bright, shining gasometer that guaranteed the citizens of Malmö that they would have electricity. Just over a century later, the building – and the whole neighbourhood – had changed. After the popular art museum Rooseum closed, the premises were offered to Moderna Museet. In 2008, It was decided that Moderna Museet in Stockholm would open a branch in Malmö, in one of Sweden’s most beautiful exhibition spaces. Once more, the old power station would be filled with art.

## Moderna Museet Malmö
### Opened on 26 December 2009
The assignment to convert the building into a more functional museum went to Tham & Videgård Hansson Arkitekter. They chose to create a new annexe – a contemporary addition to the historical building. They also changed the floor plan of the existing premises. On 26 December, 2009, Moderna Museet Malmö opened. The then curator at Dunkers Kulturhus in Helsingborg, Magnus Jensner, had been appointed director of the museum the previous year, a position he held until 1 March 2012. He was succeeded by the former curators at Moderna Museet in Stockholm, John Peter Nilsson (2012 – 2016) and Iris Müller-Westermann (2017 – 2022).
On 22 August 2022, Elisabeth Millqvist became the director of Moderna Museet Malmö. She had been the artistic director and head of operations at Wanås Konst since 2011.

## 2010s
In November 2010, Daniel Birnbaum became the new chief curator and director of Moderna Museet. Daniel Birnbaum was formerly the vice-chancellor and a professor at Städelschule in Frankfurt, Germany, and the chief curator of numerous major international exhibitions and biennials, including the Venice Biennale in 2009.
In 2011, the exhibition series “Moment” replaces the previous “The 1st at Moderna”, as a forum for smaller exhibitions dotted around the museum. That year, a comprehensive reshuffling began in the presentation of the Moderna Museet collection.
Under the umbrella banner of “Another Story”, the museum showed only photography, from the 1840s to the early 2000s, from its own collection of some 100,000 photographs. This radical re-hanging was presented in the collection galleries throughout 2011.

## 2010s
### International group exhibitions
In Stockholm, the exhibition programme in the 2010s was predominantly female: Eva Löfdahl, Eija-Liisa Ahtila, Yoko Ono, Yayoi Kusama, Marina Abramovic, Cindy Sherman and Marie-Louise Ekman were a few of the artists featured.
Among the notable international group exhibitions were “Explosion – Painting as Action”, “Pop Art Design” and “Sculpture after Sculpture”, along with mid-career exhibitions of Wolfgang Tillmans and Olafur Eliasson. In February 2012, the museum stayed open for 48 hours for the sound installation “freq_out 8”.

## 2010s
### Hilma af Klint, Hannah Ryggen & Rosemarie Trockel
Women artists were also highlighted at Moderna Museet Malmö in the 2010s, including Doris Salcedo, Tala Madani, Tora Vega Holmström, Hannah Ryggen, Rosemarie Trockel and Hilma af Klint.
In association with Moderna Museet in Stockholm, several exhibitions of works from the collection were featured, including “Supersurrealism”, “Towards a Bigger World” and “A Way of Life”, along with international group shows such as “The New Human” and solo presentations of artists such as Ragnar Kjartansson and Katarzyna Kobro & Władysław Strzemiński. One of the public favourites was “ACTIONPAINTINGBABYSPLASH!”, an experimental mixture of exhibition and creative workshop in 2015.
On 31 December 2018, Daniel Birnbaum resigned as director of Moderna Museet, and Ann-Sofi Noring took over as acting director. Noring’s directorship ended on 1 September 2019, when she was succeeded by Gitte Ørskou, who had been the director of the Kunsten Museum of Modern Art in Aalborg, Denmark, since 2009. Before that, she was the curator and chief curator of ARoS Aarhus Kunstmuseum. She had also been on several boards, and chaired the Danish Arts Foundation.

# Nan Goldin
This Will Not End Well
29.10 2022–26.2 2023
Stockholm
Nan Goldin is one of the most high-profile and controversial artists of our time. The retrospective “This Will Not End Well” is presented in six unique rooms. Experience her works as slideshows and films set to sound and music, where stories about love, intimacy, addiction, and loss take place on the screens.

Nan Goldin, Amanda at the sauna, Hotel Savoy, Berlin (1983) © Nan Goldin

# Nan Goldin
## About the exhibition
Nan Goldin has made an unforgettable mark on our time with candid and tender snapshots of intimacy and relationships, everyday life, wild parties, and the struggle between addiction and independence.
“This Will Not End Well” is the first exhibition that embraces Goldin’s original vision of how her work is to be experienced. By focusing on slideshows and video installations the exhibition goes back to the roots of Goldin’s artistic practice.
> “I have always wanted to be a filmmaker. My slideshows are films made up of stills.”  
>   
> Nan Goldin
Nan Goldin, Couple in bed, Chicago (1977) © Nan Goldin
Nan Goldin, Cookie at Tin Pan Alley, New York City (1983) © Nan Goldin

# Nan Goldin
## About the exhibition
### Breakthrough in the 1980s
Born in Washington D.C., Nan Goldin started her career in New York in the early 1980s. She presented her work in nightclubs, underground cinemas and film festivals. Live in front of an audience, she showed images organized in slideshows with multiple projectors, set to an eclectic soundtrack.
Her magnum opus work “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency”, documents Goldin’s bohemian, creative social circle and their world in Provincetown, in Lower Manhattan, Berlin, and London during the 1970s and 80s until recently.
Over the past 50 years, Goldin has produced a dozen separate slideshows with thousands of images. She has added new elements to her works over time, such as moving images, voices, and archival material.

# Nan Goldin
## Works in the exhibition
The exhibition is comprised of: “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency” (1981–2022) her magnum opus; “The Other Side” (1992– 2021) a historical portrait produced as an homage to her trans friends whom she photographed 1972–2010; “Sisters, Saints and Sibyls” (2004–2022) a testament to the trauma of families and suicide; “Fire Leap” (2010–2022) a foray into the world of children; “Memory Lost” (2019–2021) a claustrophobic journey through drug withdrawal; and “Sirens” (2019–2020) a trip into drug ecstasy.

# Nan Goldin
## Works in the exhibition
### Curator Fredrik Liew on the exhibition title:
“Hope and despair, sadness and joy, private and political struggle coexist in the exhibition. This ambiguity is also found in the exhibition’s title. “This Will Not End Well” may seem dark and foreboding but the darkness also contains ironic humor and warmth, Goldin’s characteristically unshakeable joie de vivre.”

b.1953, Washington, DC, Lives and works in New York, Paris, and Berlin
CV
First as a teenager in Boston in the 1960s, then in New York starting in the 1970s, Nan Goldin has taken intensely personal, spontaneous, sexual, and transgressive photographs of her family, friends, and lovers. In 1979 she presented her first slideshow in a New York City nightclub, and her richly colored, snap-shot-like photographs were soon heralded as a groundbreaking contribution to fine art photography. _The Ballad of Sexual Dependency_—the name she gave her ever-evolving show—eventually grew into a forty-five-minute multimedia presentation of more than 900 photographs, accompanied by a musical soundtrack, and published as an award-winning book.

Goldin’s work has been the subject of major touring retrospectives, organized in 1996 by the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York, and in 2001, by the Centre Pompidou, Paris, and Whitechapel Art Gallery, London. Her work has been exhibited widely, often in site-specific installations: her video piece _Sisters, Saints, and Sibyls_ was presented at La Chapelle de la Salpêtrière for a 1-month run; her _Scopophilia_ exhibition was part of Patrice Chéreau’s special program at the Louvre; and in 2019, an exhibition of site-responsive photographs opened at Versailles. _The Ballad of Sexual Dependency_ was presented live in Turbine Hall at Tate Modern, London, in 2008, and the slideshow was installed in the exhibition _Here is Every. Four Decades of Contemporary Art_ at The Museum of Modern Art, New York, September 2008 to March 2009. In 2017, MoMA presented the piece in its original 35mm format. In 2022, Moderna Museet in Stockholm debuted an internationally traveling exhibition of six slideshows and video installations spanning her entire career, tiled “This Will Not End Well.” Her slideshow _Stendhal Syndrome_ was featured at Rencontres d’Arles in France in 2025.

> Nan Goldin
b.1953, Washington, DC, Lives and works in New York, Paris, and Berlin
CV
First as a teenager in Boston in the 1960s, then in New York starting in the 1970s, Nan Goldin has taken intensely personal, spontaneous, sexual, and transgressive photographs of her family, friends, and lovers. In 1979 she presented her first slideshow in a New York City nightclub, and her richly colored, snap-shot-like photographs were soon heralded as a groundbreaking contribution to fine art photography. _The Ballad of Sexual Dependency_—the name she gave her ever-evolving show—eventually grew into a forty-five-minute multimedia presentation of more than 900 photographs, accompanied by a musical soundtrack, and published as an award-winning book.

Goldin’s work has been the subject of major touring retrospectives, organized in 1996 by the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York, and in 2001, by the Centre Pompidou, Paris, and Whitechapel Art Gallery, London. Her work has been exhibited widely, often in site-specific installations: her video piece _Sisters, Saints, and Sibyls_ was presented at La Chapelle de la Salpêtrière for a 1-month run; her _Scopophilia_ exhibition was part of Patrice Chéreau’s special program at the Louvre; and in 2019, an exhibition of site-responsive photographs opened at Versailles. _The Ballad of Sexual Dependency_ was presented live in Turbine Hall at Tate Modern, London, in 2008, and the slideshow was installed in the exhibition _Here is Every. Four Decades of Contemporary Art_ at The Museum of Modern Art, New York, September 2008 to March 2009. In 2017, MoMA presented the piece in its original 35mm format. In 2022, Moderna Museet in Stockholm debuted an internationally traveling exhibition of six slideshows and video installations spanning her entire career, tiled “This Will Not End Well.” Her slideshow _Stendhal Syndrome_ was featured at Rencontres d’Arles in France in 2025.

# Nan Goldin
## About the exhibition
Nan Goldin has made an unforgettable mark on our time with candid and tender snapshots of intimacy and relationships, everyday life, wild parties, and the struggle between addiction and independence.
“This Will Not End Well” is the first exhibition that embraces Goldin’s original vision of how her work is to be experienced. By focusing on slideshows and video installations the exhibition goes back to the roots of Goldin’s artistic practice.
> “I have always wanted to be a filmmaker. My slideshows are films made up of stills.”  
>   
> Nan Goldin
Nan Goldin, Couple in bed, Chicago (1977) © Nan Goldin
Nan Goldin, Cookie at Tin Pan Alley, New York City (1983) © Nan Goldin
texts.4:
# Nan Goldin
## About the exhibition
### Breakthrough in the 1980s
Born in Washington D.C., Nan Goldin started her career in New York in the early 1980s. She presented her work in nightclubs, underground cinemas and film festivals. Live in front of an audience, she showed images organized in slideshows with multiple projectors, set to an eclectic soundtrack.
Her magnum opus work “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency”, documents Goldin’s bohemian, creative social circle and their world in Provincetown, in Lower Manhattan, Berlin, and London during the 1970s and 80s until recently.
Over the past 50 years, Goldin has produced a dozen separate slideshows with thousands of images. She has added new elements to her works over time, such as moving images, voices, and archival material.
texts.5:
# Nan Goldin
## Works in the exhibition
The exhibition is comprised of: “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency” (1981–2022) her magnum opus; “The Other Side” (1992– 2021) a historical portrait produced as an homage to her trans friends whom she photographed 1972–2010; “Sisters, Saints and Sibyls” (2004–2022) a testament to the trauma of families and suicide; “Fire Leap” (2010–2022) a foray into the world of children; “Memory Lost” (2019–2021) a claustrophobic journey through drug withdrawal; and “Sirens” (2019–2020) a trip into drug ecstasy.
texts.6:
# Nan Goldin
## Works in the exhibition
### Curator Fredrik Liew on the exhibition title:
“Hope and despair, sadness and joy, private and political struggle coexist in the exhibition. This ambiguity is also found in the exhibition’s title. “This Will Not End Well” may seem dark and foreboding but the darkness also contains ironic humor and warmth, Goldin’s characteristically unshakeable joie de vivre.”

Goldin’s work has been the subject of major touring retrospectives, organized in 1996 by the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York, and in 2001, by the Centre Pompidou, Paris, and Whitechapel Art Gallery, London. Her work has been exhibited widely, often in site-specific installations: her video piece _Sisters, Saints, and Sibyls_ was presented at La Chapelle de la Salpêtrière for a 1-month run; her _Scopophilia_ exhibition was part of Patrice Chéreau’s special program at the Louvre; and in 2019, an exhibition of site-responsive photographs opened at Versailles. _The Ballad of Sexual Dependency_ was presented live in Turbine Hall at Tate Modern, London, in 2008, and the slideshow was installed in the exhibition _Here is Every. Four Decades of Contemporary Art_ at The Museum of Modern Art, New York, September 2008 to March 2009. In 2017, MoMA presented the piece in its original 35mm format. In 2022, Moderna Museet in Stockholm debuted an internationally traveling exhibition of six slideshows and video installations spanning her entire career, tiled “This Will Not End Well.” Her slideshow _Stendhal Syndrome_ was featured at Rencontres d’Arles in France in 2025.

# Nan Goldin
## About the exhibition
Nan Goldin has made an unforgettable mark on our time with candid and tender snapshots of intimacy and relationships, everyday life, wild parties, and the struggle between addiction and independence.
“This Will Not End Well” is the first exhibition that embraces Goldin’s original vision of how her work is to be experienced. By focusing on slideshows and video installations the exhibition goes back to the roots of Goldin’s artistic practice.
> “I have always wanted to be a filmmaker. My slideshows are films made up of stills.”  
>   
> Nan Goldin
Nan Goldin, Couple in bed, Chicago (1977) © Nan Goldin
Nan Goldin, Cookie at Tin Pan Alley, New York City (1983) © Nan Goldin

# Nan Goldin
## About the exhibition
### Breakthrough in the 1980s
Born in Washington D.C., Nan Goldin started her career in New York in the early 1980s. She presented her work in nightclubs, underground cinemas and film festivals. Live in front of an audience, she showed images organized in slideshows with multiple projectors, set to an eclectic soundtrack.
Her magnum opus work “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency”, documents Goldin’s bohemian, creative social circle and their world in Provincetown, in Lower Manhattan, Berlin, and London during the 1970s and 80s until recently.
Over the past 50 years, Goldin has produced a dozen separate slideshows with thousands of images. She has added new elements to her works over time, such as moving images, voices, and archival material.

# Nan Goldin
## Works in the exhibition
The exhibition is comprised of: “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency” (1981–2022) her magnum opus; “The Other Side” (1992– 2021) a historical portrait produced as an homage to her trans friends whom she photographed 1972–2010; “Sisters, Saints and Sibyls” (2004–2022) a testament to the trauma of families and suicide; “Fire Leap” (2010–2022) a foray into the world of children; “Memory Lost” (2019–2021) a claustrophobic journey through drug withdrawal; and “Sirens” (2019–2020) a trip into drug ecstasy.

# Nan Goldin
## Works in the exhibition
### Curator Fredrik Liew on the exhibition title:
“Hope and despair, sadness and joy, private and political struggle coexist in the exhibition. This ambiguity is also found in the exhibition’s title. “This Will Not End Well” may seem dark and foreboding but the darkness also contains ironic humor and warmth, Goldin’s characteristically unshakeable joie de vivre.”

Francesco Vezzoli was born in 1971, in Brescia, Italy.He studied at the Central St. Martin’s School of Art in London.
One of the most successful contemporary Italian artists,his work can be described as a series of strong allegories about contemporary culture, with a rich subtext of elaborate references involving video installations, petit-point embroideries, photography, live performances, media experiments and -most recently- classical sculpture.
His works have been selected four times at the Venice Biennale: at the 49th, 51st and 52nd art editions held in 2001, 2005 and 2007, respectively, and at the 2014 Architecture Biennial. His works have also been featured in other international exhibitions such as the Whitney Biennial 2006, the 26th Biennale in Sao Paulo, the 6th International Biennale in Istanbul and Performa (2007 and 2015).
In 2017, he produced a live opera performance for the 40th anniversary of Centre Pompidou and in 2019 he brought the exhibition 'Huysmans Critique d’Art: De Degas à Grünewald, sous le Regard de Francesco Vezzoli'at Musée d’Orsay in Paris.In 2021, Vezzoli worked with Fondazione Brescia Musei on the exhibition project 'Palcoscenici Archeologici', and again that year he was the protagonist of the 'Francesco Vezzoli in Florence'exhibition, with two new sculptures in Piazza della Signoria and Palazzo Vecchio in Florence. This made him the first living Italian artist to produce a site-specific work for Piazza della Signoria, creating an interaction between contemporary art and the city’s historical heritage.
His latest exhibitions, 'VITA DVLCIS: fear and desire in the Roman Empire'at Palazzo delle Esposizioni in Rome and 'Museums of Tears'at Museo Correr in Venice, allowed him to relate his recent artworks, respectively, to Roman archaeological masterpieces and Italian historical paintings.

He has also held solo shows around the world in venues such as the New Museum of Contemporary Art, New York; Tate Modern, London; MOCA, Los Angeles; MoMA PS1 in New York; MAXXI, Museo Nazionale delle Arti del XXI secolo, Rome; Moderna Museet, Stockholm; Kunsthalle, Wien;Pinakothek der Moderne, Munich; Museum Ludwig, Cologne; The Garage CCC, Moscow;The Power Plant, Toronto;Jeu de Paume, Paris; Castello di Rivoli Museo d’Arte Contemporanea, Turin; Museo Serralves, Porto; Fondazione Prada, Milan; Le Consortium, Dijon;Fondazione Museion in Bolzano and NMNM - Nouveau Musée National de Monaco.
His work has been shown, among others, at: the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, the Whitechapel Art Gallery in London, le Grand Palais in Paris, Museo del Novecento in Milan, Palazzo Grassi - François Pinault Foundation in Venice, Fabric Workshop and Museum in Philadelphia, Witte de With Center for Contemporary Art in Rotterdam, the Migros Museum in Zurich,Neues Museum in Weimer,Pirelli Hangar Bicocca in Milan and Musée National Picasso in Paris.

Francesco Vezzoli was born in 1971, in Brescia, Italy.He studied at the Central St. Martin’s School of Art in London.
One of the most successful contemporary Italian artists,his work can be described as a series of strong allegories about contemporary culture, with a rich subtext of elaborate references involving video installations, petit-point embroideries, photography, live performances, media experiments and -most recently- classical sculpture.
His works have been selected four times at the Venice Biennale: at the 49th, 51st and 52nd art editions held in 2001, 2005 and 2007, respectively, and at the 2014 Architecture Biennial. His works have also been featured in other international exhibitions such as the Whitney Biennial 2006, the 26th Biennale in Sao Paulo, the 6th International Biennale in Istanbul and Performa (2007 and 2015).
In 2017, he produced a live opera performance for the 40th anniversary of Centre Pompidou and in 2019 he brought the exhibition 'Huysmans Critique d’Art: De Degas à Grünewald, sous le Regard de Francesco Vezzoli'at Musée d’Orsay in Paris.In 2021, Vezzoli worked with Fondazione Brescia Musei on the exhibition project 'Palcoscenici Archeologici', and again that year he was the protagonist of the 'Francesco Vezzoli in Florence'exhibition, with two new sculptures in Piazza della Signoria and Palazzo Vecchio in Florence. This made him the first living Italian artist to produce a site-specific work for Piazza della Signoria, creating an interaction between contemporary art and the city’s historical heritage.
His latest exhibitions, 'VITA DVLCIS: fear and desire in the Roman Empire'at Palazzo delle Esposizioni in Rome and 'Museums of Tears'at Museo Correr in Venice, allowed him to relate his recent artworks, respectively, to Roman archaeological masterpieces and Italian historical paintings.

He has also held solo shows around the world in venues such as the New Museum of Contemporary Art, New York; Tate Modern, London; MOCA, Los Angeles; MoMA PS1 in New York; MAXXI, Museo Nazionale delle Arti del XXI secolo, Rome; Moderna Museet, Stockholm; Kunsthalle, Wien;Pinakothek der Moderne, Munich; Museum Ludwig, Cologne; The Garage CCC, Moscow;The Power Plant, Toronto;Jeu de Paume, Paris; Castello di Rivoli Museo d’Arte Contemporanea, Turin; Museo Serralves, Porto; Fondazione Prada, Milan; Le Consortium, Dijon;Fondazione Museion in Bolzano and NMNM - Nouveau Musée National de Monaco.
His work has been shown, among others, at: the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, the Whitechapel Art Gallery in London, le Grand Palais in Paris, Museo del Novecento in Milan, Palazzo Grassi - François Pinault Foundation in Venice, Fabric Workshop and Museum in Philadelphia, Witte de With Center for Contemporary Art in Rotterdam, the Migros Museum in Zurich,Neues Museum in Weimer,Pirelli Hangar Bicocca in Milan and Musée National Picasso in Paris.

Title: Francesco Vezzoli: Artist Overview - Almine Rech
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Francesco Vezzoli was born in 1971, in Brescia, Italy.He studied at the Central St. Martin’s School of Art in London.
One of the most successful contemporary Italian artists,his work can be described as a series of strong allegories about contemporary culture, with a rich subtext of elaborate references involving video installations, petit-point embroideries, photography, live performances, media experiments and -most recently- classical sculpture.
His works have been selected four times at the Venice Biennale: at the 49th, 51st and 52nd art editions held in 2001, 2005 and 2007, respectively, and at the 2014 Architecture Biennial. His works have also been featured in other international exhibitions such as the Whitney Biennial 2006, the 26th Biennale in Sao Paulo, the 6th International Biennale in Istanbul and Performa (2007 and 2015).
In 2017, he produced a live opera performance for the 40th anniversary of Centre Pompidou and in 2019 he brought the exhibition 'Huysmans Critique d’Art: De Degas à Grünewald, sous le Regard de Francesco Vezzoli'at Musée d’Orsay in Paris.In 2021, Vezzoli worked with Fondazione Brescia Musei on the exhibition project 'Palcoscenici Archeologici', and again that year he was the protagonist of the 'Francesco Vezzoli in Florence'exhibition, with two new sculptures in Piazza della Signoria and Palazzo Vecchio in Florence. This made him the first living Italian artist to produce a site-specific work for Piazza della Signoria, creating an interaction between contemporary art and the city’s historical heritage.
His latest exhibitions, 'VITA DVLCIS: fear and desire in the Roman Empire'at Palazzo delle Esposizioni in Rome and 'Museums of Tears'at Museo Correr in Venice, allowed him to relate his recent artworks, respectively, to Roman archaeological masterpieces and Italian historical paintings.

He has also held solo shows around the world in venues such as the New Museum of Contemporary Art, New York; Tate Modern, London; MOCA, Los Angeles; MoMA PS1 in New York; MAXXI, Museo Nazionale delle Arti del XXI secolo, Rome; Moderna Museet, Stockholm; Kunsthalle, Wien;Pinakothek der Moderne, Munich; Museum Ludwig, Cologne; The Garage CCC, Moscow;The Power Plant, Toronto;Jeu de Paume, Paris; Castello di Rivoli Museo d’Arte Contemporanea, Turin; Museo Serralves, Porto; Fondazione Prada, Milan; Le Consortium, Dijon;Fondazione Museion in Bolzano and NMNM - Nouveau Musée National de Monaco.
His work has been shown, among others, at: the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, the Whitechapel Art Gallery in London, le Grand Palais in Paris, Museo del Novecento in Milan, Palazzo Grassi - François Pinault Foundation in Venice, Fabric Workshop and Museum in Philadelphia, Witte de With Center for Contemporary Art in Rotterdam, the Migros Museum in Zurich,Neues Museum in Weimer,Pirelli Hangar Bicocca in Milan and Musée National Picasso in Paris.

Photographer Ikram Abdulkadir (born 1995) has attracted a lot of attention in recent years. In the upper galleries, her work and that of Deborah Turbeville are presented in separate exhibitions, yet in dialogue with one another.

## About this exhibition
Moderna Museet Malmö presents two parallel exhibitions: “Deborah Turbeville – Photocollage” and “Ikram Abdulkadir – Soft Focus”. Installed side by side on Level 2, the exhibitions each take fashion and portrait photography as their point of departure. In both artists’ practices, people are at the centre – in images marked by presence, atmosphere, and a sense of timelessness.
In the encounter between Deborah Turbeville and Ikram Abdulkadir, both similarities and differences emerge. While Turbeville worked with staged environments and a deliberate aesthetic, Abdulkadir departs from the intimate and the everyday. At the same time, a shared sensibility becomes visible – a gaze that lingers, a resistance to fixed meanings, and a desire to make space for what otherwise remains unspoken. Both artists’ practices can be related to pictorialism, an early movement in art photography in which images are often softly focused and approach the painterly. In Turbeville’s work, this is evident in her manipulated photographs and photocollages; in Abdulkadir’s, in her way of working with colour, form, and light and shadow.
Ikram Abdulkadir (born 1995) began photographing in high school and published her images on the Instagram account @ikramianism, which quickly led to attention and several fashion and portrait commissions. Since her debut, she has had solo exhibitions in Malmö, Stockholm, Norrköping, and Copenhagen, and in the summer of 2023 she participated in the group exhibition “Søsterskap – Contemporary Nordic Photography” at the international photography festival Les Rencontres de la Photographie in Arles, France. Ikram Abdulkadir is represented in the Moderna Museet Collection.
For the exhibition “Soft Focus”, Abdulkadir has revisited her extensive archive, which today contains thousands of images, selecting both new and earlier works that play off one another and highlight central themes in her practice. In many of the motifs, we catch glimpses of family and friends, both at home and out in the city’s streets and squares. She uses a colour palette that ranges from muted greens, blues, and browns to stronger signature tones of red, pink, and purple. Technical experiments, such as double exposures and overexposures, are employed to make the motifs both enigmatic and compelling.
